# The ATM-E6AP-MASTL axis mediates DNA damage checkpoint recovery

- Feifei Wang<sup>1</sup>
- Xin Li<sup>1</sup> ([ORCID: 0000-0002-5200-3858](https://orcid.org/0000-0002-5200-3858))

## Abstract

Checkpoint activation after DNA damage causes a transient cell cycle arrest by suppressing cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs). However, it remains largely elusive how cell cycle recovery is initiated after DNA damage. In this study, we discovered the upregulated protein level of MASTL kinase hours after DNA damage. MASTL promotes cell cycle progression by preventing PP2A/B55-catalyzed dephosphorylation of CDK substrates. DNA damage-induced MASTL upregulation was caused by decreased protein degradation, and was unique among mitotic kinases. We identified E6AP as the E3 ubiquitin ligase that mediated MASTL degradation. MASTL degradation was inhibited upon DNA damage as a result of the dissociation of E6AP from MASTL. E6AP depletion reduced DNA damage signaling, and promoted cell cycle recovery from the DNA damage checkpoint, in a MASTL-dependent manner. Furthermore, we found that E6AP was phosphorylated at Ser-218 by ATM after DNA damage and that this phosphorylation was required for its dissociation from MASTL, the stabilization of MASTL, and the timely recovery of cell cycle progression. Together, our data revealed that ATM/ATR-dependent signaling, while activating the DNA damage checkpoint, also initiates cell cycle recovery from the arrest. Consequently, this results in a timer-like mechanism that ensures the transient nature of the DNA damage checkpoint.

## Introduction

DNA damage activates a wide range of cellular responses, including DNA repair, cell cycle checkpoints, and cell death. Collectively defined as the DNA damage response (DDR), these mechanisms ensure genomic integrity and prevent progression of cancer, aging, and other diseases (Ciccia and Elledge, 2010; Jackson and Bartek, 2009; Lou and Chen, 2005). Among these DDR pathways, the DNA damage checkpoint temporally halts the progression of the cell cycle, to facilitate DNA repair and avoid detrimental accumulation of DNA damage. The DNA damage checkpoint can act at multiple stages of the cell cycle to impede DNA replication and block mitotic entry. Initiation of the DNA damage checkpoint signaling relies on two phosphoinositide 3 kinase-related protein kinases, ataxia-telangiectasia mutated (ATM), ATM and RAD3-related (ATR). Upon DNA damage, ATM and ATR phosphorylate and activate checkpoint kinases CHK1 and CHK2, which, in turn, inhibit CDC25 to prevent activation of cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs) (Shiloh, 2003; Zhou and Elledge, 2000).

How does the cell initiate cell cycle recovery after DNA damage is an important, yet largely unanswered, question. Distinct from the simplistic view that the cell cycle resumes passively following the repair of DNA damage and decay of checkpoint signaling, recovery from the DNA damage checkpoint is likely an active and regulated process (Bartek and Lukas, 2007; Clémenson and Marsolier-Kergoat, 2009). For example, Polo-like kinase 1 (PLK1) and other cell cycle kinases can facilitate the deactivation of DNA damage signaling and resumption of cell cycle progression (Alvarez-Fernández et al., 2010; Macůrek et al., 2008; Mamely et al., 2006; Peng, 2013; Peschiaroli et al., 2006; van Vugt et al., 2004a). Furthermore, it has been observed in yeast, frog, and mammalian cells that the cell cycle can be restarted without completion of DNA repair, a phenomenon defined as adaptation (Bartek and Lukas, 2007; Clémenson and Marsolier-Kergoat, 2009; Syljuåsen, 2007; Toczyski et al., 1997; van Vugt and Medema, 2004b; Yoo et al., 2004). Aside from senescence and other types of permanent cell cycle withdrawal, the DNA damage checkpoint-mediated cell cycle arrest is transient, raising the question about mechanisms that mediate the timely initiation of DNA damage checkpoint recovery.

Microtubule-associated serine/threonine kinase-like (MASTL, also known as Greatwall) has been characterized as an important regulator of mitosis. Like CDK1 and other mitotic kinases, MASTL is activated during mitotic entry, and the kinase activity of MASTL promotes mitosis, although mitotic entry is still permitted in mammalian cells depleted of MASTL (Archambault et al., 2007; Blake-Hodek et al., 2012; Castilho et al., 2009; Peng and Maller, 2010; Vigneron et al., 2011; Voets and Wolthuis, 2010; Wang et al., 2016; Yu et al., 2004; Yu et al., 2006). Upon activation, MASTL phosphorylates α-endosulfine (ENSA) and cyclic AMP-regulated 19 kDa phosphoprotein (ARPP19) which then inhibit PP2A/B55 (protein phosphatase 2A/B55 targeting subunit). Because PP2A/B55 functions as the principal phosphatase catalyzing the dephosphorylation of CDK substrates, the coordination between the kinase activity of MASTL with that of CDK1 enables substrate phosphorylation and mitotic progression (Castilho et al., 2009; Gharbi-Ayachi et al., 2010; Mochida et al., 2009; Mochida et al., 2010; Vigneron et al., 2009).

Interestingly, in addition to its mitotic function, MASTL is also required for cell cycle recovery from the DNA damage checkpoint in Xenopus egg extracts (Medema, 2010; Peng et al., 2011; Peng et al., 2010). Addition of MASTL in extracts facilitated, and depletion of MASTL hindered, DNA damage checkpoint recovery, as evidenced by both mitotic phosphorylation of CDK substrates and de-activation of checkpoint signaling (Peng et al., 2011; Peng et al., 2010). Consistently, ectopic expression of MASTL in human cells promoted cell proliferation under DNA damage (Wang et al., 2014; Wong et al., 2016). In this study, we discovered the protein stabilization of MASTL post DNA damage, identified E6 associated protein (E6AP) as the underlying E3 ubiquitin ligase mediating MASTL proteolysis, and delineated ATM-mediated E6AP phosphorylation as a mechanism to initiate DNA damage checkpoint recovery.

## Results

### MASTL expression is upregulated after DNA damage

While investigating the role of MASTL in cell cycle regulation and DDR, we observed unexpected upregulation of MASTL protein levels in cells treated with DNA damage. As shown in Figure 1A–C, MASTL upregulation was evident in HEK293 cells treated with doxorubicin (DOX), hydroxyurea (HU), or camptothecin (CPT), generally within hours post treatment. MASTL accumulation was also confirmed in SCC38 cells treated with HU or ionizing radiation (IR, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B), and HeLa cells treated with DOX or HU (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C-E). DNA damage-induced MASTL upregulation was consistent with the activation of ATM/ATR signaling (Figure 1D and E), and was not likely to be caused by the completion of DNA repair, as judged by the phosphorylation of replication protein A (RPA, Figure 1A–D), H2AX and ATM/ATR substrates (Figure 1D and E). In contrast to MASTL, DNA damage did not induce upregulation of other cell cycle kinases that mediate mitotic progression, including CDK1/cyclin B, Aurora A, Aurora B, and PLK1, in HeLa cells treated with DOX (Figure 1F), HU (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A), or SCC38 cells with HU (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B). Furthermore, HU-induced MASTL upregulation was abrogated when cells were treated with caffeine (Figure 1G), indicating that DNA damage-induced ATM/ATR activation acted upstream of MASTL upregulation.

### MASTL upregulation after DNA damage is caused by protein stabilization

We did not observe a substantial increase in MASTL RNA transcripts, suggesting MASTL regulation at the post-translational level (Figure 2A). Along this line, exogenous MASTL expressed from a different promoter underwent a similar pattern of upregulation after HU, as shown by immunoblotting (Figure 2B), and by direct fluorescence (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B). Like the endogenous MASTL, accumulation of exogenous MASTL occurred concurrently with activation of DNA damage signaling, measured by phosphorylation of ATM/ATR substrates (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-C). These observations prompted us to examine the possibility that DNA damage increased the protein stability of MASTL. Indeed, CPT treatment in HeLa cells increased the protein stability of MASTL, as evaluated by the rate of protein degradation in the presence of cycloheximide (CHX), a protein synthesis inhibitor (Figure 2C). Consistently, HU treatment prolonged the half-life of MASTL protein in SCC38 and HEK293 cells (Figure 2D–F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D and E).

### E6AP associates with MASTL

To elucidate MASTL regulation via protein stability, we sought to identify the ubiquitin ligase that mediates MASTL proteolysis. We previously performed a proteomic analysis of proteins associated with MASTL (Ren et al., 2017), and revealed E6AP as a potential binding partner of MASTL. E6AP is encoded by gene ubiquitin-protein ligase E3A (UBE3A), and is the founding member of the HECT (homologous to E6AP C-terminus)-domain ubiquitin ligase family (Bernassola et al., 2008; Scheffner and Kumar, 2014). The association between E6AP and MASTL was confirmed by co-immunoprecipitation (Figure 3A), and by pulldown of MASTL in HeLa cell lysate using recombinant E6AP (Figure 3B). A direct interaction between purified E6AP and MASTL proteins was also evident (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A). Further analyses using various segments of MASTL showed that the N-terminal region of MASTL mediated E6AP interaction in HeLa cells and Xenopus egg extracts (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, Figure 3C). On the other hand, the N-terminus of E6AP co-immunoprecipitated MASTL (Figure 3D); the MASTL-binding region was further mapped to aa 208–280 within the N-terminus of E6AP (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C). Taken together, our data characterized the MASTL-E6AP association which was likely mediated via direct protein interaction, although the potential involvement of additional binding partners was not excluded.

### E6AP mediates MASTL ubiquitination and degradation

To determine the potential role of E6AP in MASTL regulation, we depleted E6AP in cells using an siRNA and assessed the mRNA and protein levels of MASTL. As shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, E6AP depletion led to an increased level of MASTL protein, without significant change in the MASTL mRNA level. Ectopic expression of E6AP reduced MASTL expression, as shown by immunoblotting (Figure 4B) and immunofluorescence (IF) (Figure 4C). Consistently, CRISPR-Cas9-mediated gene deletion of E6AP also augmented MASTL level, in a manner that was reversed by re-expression of exogenous E6AP (Figure 4D). E6AP depletion increased, and overexpression reduced, the protein stability of MASTL (Figure 4E and F). Furthermore, E6AP depletion disrupted MASTL ubiquitination in HeLa cells (Figure 4G), indicating that E6AP mediated the ubiquitination of MASTL. Consistently, E6AP depletion did not further increase MASTL level in cells treated with MG132 to suppress proteasome-mediated protein degradation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B). An in vitro ubiquitination assay also confirmed MASTL as an effective substrate of E6AP (Figure 4H). MASTL ubiquitination was specifically mediated by E6AP in the assay (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C); the MASTL mutant deleted of the E6AP-binding motif was not ubiquitinated (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D). Together, these data established E6AP as a key modulator of MASTL stability.

### E6AP depletion facilitates DNA damage recovery via MASTL

A potential consequence of MASTL accumulation after DNA damage is cell cycle recovery, given the established role of MASTL in promoting cell cycle progression. To analyze cell cycle progression following etoposide (ETO) treatment and release, we quantified mitotic cells that exhibited chromosome condensation and activation of Aurora A/B/C kinases (Figure 5A). MASTL depletion substantially hindered DNA damage recovery, whereas E6AP knockout (KO) accelerated mitotic entry after DNA damage (Figure 5A). The recovery of mitotic entry in E6AP KO cells was disrupted by MASTL downregulation, indicating its dependence on MASTL (Figure 5A). To further study DNA damage recovery, we profiled the cell cycle progression of cells released from HU treatment (Figure 5B). MASTL depletion caused prolonged cell cycle arrest; loss of E6AP promoted cell cycle recovery; and suppression of MASTL in E6AP-deleted cells abrogated cell cycle progression (Figure 5B). By comparison, MASTL knockdown did not significantly disrupt cell proliferation under the unperturbed condition (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).

Interestingly, KO of E6AP in HEK293 cells reduced DNA damage checkpoint signaling, measured by phosphorylation of SMC1, CHK1, CHK2, H2AX, and pan-ATM/ATR substrates after DOX treatment (Figure 5C), and by phosphorylation of pan-ATM/ATR substrates after ETO (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B). Interestingly, ATM/ATR-mediated substrate phosphorylation in E6AP KO cells was also restored by MASTL depletion, indicating that E6AP promoted DNA damage checkpoint signaling by counteracting MASTL (Figure 5E).

### E6AP and MASTL association is regulated by ATM/ATR-mediated DNA damage signaling

Prompted by the findings that E6AP mediated the proteolysis of MASTL and that MASTL protein accumulated following DNA damage, we asked if the association between E6AP and MASTL was impacted by DNA damage. Interestingly, co-immunoprecipitation of E6AP with CPF-MASTL was profoundly disrupted by HU treatment (Figure 6A). This loss of E6AP and MASTL association was a result of active DNA damage signaling, as inhibition of ATM/ATR by caffeine preserved this protein association in the presence of HU (Figure 6B). These lines of evidence pointed to a model that DNA damage-induced ATM/ATR activation disrupts E6AP association with MASTL, subsequently leading to reduced MASTL degradation and increased MASTL protein accumulation.

### ATM/ATR mediates E6AP S218 phosphorylation to modulate E6AP and MASTL association

ATM/ATR phosphorylates numerous substrates to regulate their functions after DNA damage. These kinases typically target serine or threonine residues followed by glutamine (S/TQ). E6AP possesses a single evolutionally conserved serine, Ser-218 in humans, as a potential consensus site of ATM/ATR-mediated phosphorylation (Figure 7A). E6AP Ser-218 phosphorylation was also documented in multiple proteomic databases (Beli et al., 2012; Franz-Wachtel et al., 2012; Kettenbach et al., 2011; Klammer et al., 2012; Matsuoka et al., 2007; Olsen et al., 2010; Schweppe et al., 2013; Weber et al., 2012). We generated a phospho-specific antibody for this residue, and observed the induction of Ser-218 phosphorylation after HU (Figure 7B), or DOX treatment (Figure 7C). This phospho-signal was absent in E6AP KO cells (Figure 7B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A), and was diminished with S218A mutation (Figure 7E), confirming its specificity. Inhibition of ATM using a selective kinase inhibitor reduced E6AP Ser-218 phosphorylation after DOX treatment in both HeLa and HEK293 cells (Figure 7C, Figure 7—figure supplement 1B). ATM was also the primary kinase to mediate E6AP Ser-218 phosphorylation in response to HU (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).

## Discussion

In this study, we identified E6AP as the underlying E3 ubiquitin ligase that mediated the ubiquitination and degradation of MASTL. Compared to the function of MASTL, regulation of MASTL is relatively underinvestigated. Previous studies illustrated mechanisms that modulated the phosphorylation and subcellular localization of MASTL during cell cycle progression (Castro and Lorca, 2018). We reported here that DNA damage disrupted E6AP and MASTL association, leading to increased MASTL protein stability and accumulation of MASTL protein. Because MASTL promotes the phosphorylation of CDK substrates by inhibiting the counteracting phosphatase PP2A/B55, this fashion of MASTL upregulation can re-activate cell cycle progression while CDK activities are restrained by the DNA damage checkpoint (Figure 9). By comparison, other cell cycle kinases that promote mitotic progression, including CDK1/cyclin B, Aurora A/B, and PLK1, did not exhibit this pattern of DNA damage-induced upregulation.

![Figure 9.](https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/86976/elife-86976-fig9-v1.jpg)

**Figure 9.:** DNA damage induces ATM/ATR activation and checkpoint signaling. At this stage (the initial DNA damage sensing/signaling), MASTL expression is normal (not yet upregulated). Activated ATM/ATR also phosphorylates E6AP Ser-218, leading to the dissociation of E6AP from MASTL and reduced MASTL degradation. The subsequent accumulation of MASTL, at upregulated levels several hours after DNA damage, promotes de-activation of the DNA damage checkpoint and initiates cell cycle resumption by inhibiting dephosphorylation of cyclin-dependent kinase (CDK) substrates.

E6AP, also known as UBE3A, is the prototype of the E3 ligase subfamily containing a C-terminal HECT domain. Mutations of E6AP cause Angelman syndrome, a debilitating neurological disorder in humans (Bernassola et al., 2008; Buiting et al., 2016; Levav-Cohen et al., 2012; Sell and Margolis, 2015; Wolyniec et al., 2013). E6AP and other HECT-containing E3 ligases are emerging as potential etiological factors and drug targets in cancer (Bernassola et al., 2008; Scheffner and Kumar, 2014; Yu et al., 2020). Interestingly, mouse embryo fibroblasts lacking E6AP escaped replicative senescence, proliferated under stress conditions, supported anchorage-independent growth, and enhanced tumor growth in vivo (Levav-Cohen et al., 2012; Wolyniec et al., 2013). These phenotypes are not well explained in the context of known substrates of E6AP (Sell and Margolis, 2015), but can be potentially attributed to MASTL upregulation, as characterized in our current study. E6AP binds MASTL via its N-terminal domain, and mediates MASTL ubiquitination and degradation. The function of E6AP in the DNA damage checkpoint via MASTL modulation suggests E6AP as a DDR factor and a potential tumor suppressor.

ATM/ATR phosphorylates a myriad of substrates to promote DNA repair and activate the cell cycle checkpoints (Flynn and Zou, 2011; Shiloh, 2003). We found that MASTL accumulation after DNA damage was disrupted by inhibition of ATM/ATR, suggesting that ATM/ATR modulated MASTL proteolysis. Our study further revealed that ATM phosphorylated E6AP at Ser-218, leading to E6AP dissociation from MASTL and the subsequent MASTL stabilization. Our functional characterization of E6AP Ser-218 is interesting, as phosphorylation of this residue has been detected in numerous proteomic studies as a modification induced by DNA damage (Beli et al., 2012; Matsuoka et al., 2007), mitosis (Franz-Wachtel et al., 2012; Kettenbach et al., 2011; Olsen et al., 2010), or cancer progression (Klammer et al., 2012; Schweppe et al., 2013; Weber et al., 2012).

Our results suggest that ATM/ATR, while important for the activation of the DNA damage checkpoint, also engages a mechanism to initiate cell cycle recovery (Figure 9). This mechanism at least partially answers the puzzling question of how cell cycle recovery is initiated from the state of the DNA damage checkpoint. The DNA damage checkpoint targets cell cycle kinases to halt the cell cycle; on the other hand, the re-activation of CDK, PLK1, MASTL, and other cell cycle kinases promotes the de-activation of DNA damage checkpoint signaling and cell cycle resumption (Peng, 2013). For example, PLK1 and CDK can mediate the phosphorylation of DDR factors to suppress DNA damage checkpoint signaling (Alvarez-Fernández et al., 2010; Macůrek et al., 2008; Mamely et al., 2006; Peschiaroli et al., 2006; van Vugt et al., 2004a). Cell cycle kinases are known to coordinate with each other in positive feedback reactions to achieve full activation and bring about mitosis. We speculate that, in the case of DNA damage recovery, ATM-mediated MASTL upregulation may provide an initial signal to trigger these positive feedback reactions, ultimately shifting the balance from cell cycle arrest to recovery. Of note, this timer-like mechanism can contribute to the transient nature of the DNA damage checkpoint, as observed in yeast, frog, and mammalian cells (Bartek and Lukas, 2007; Clémenson and Marsolier-Kergoat, 2009; Syljuåsen, 2007; van Vugt et al., 2004a; Yoo et al., 2004). In comparison to the recovery stage, the expression level of MASTL is not upregulated during the activation stage of the DNA damage checkpoint, allowing efficient checkpoint activation. The subsequent impact of MASTL upregulation on promoting checkpoint recovery and cell cycle progression can be attributed to inhibition of PP2A/B55, although the potential involvement of additional mechanisms is not excluded. Finally, the resumption of the cell cycle after DNA damage is a potentially vital process that enables tumor cell progression and treatment evasion. MASTL kinase has emerged as an important factor of tumorigenesis and treatment resistance in multiple types of cancer (Fatima et al., 2020; Marzec and Burgess, 2018; Wang et al., 2014). Thus, future studies built upon our current findings may shed new light on cancer resistance and identify new anti-cancer drug targets to enhance treatment outcome.

Immunoblotting, IF, and immunoprecipitation (IP) were performed as previously described (Wang et al., 2019). Cytostatic factor extracts were prepared as described previously (Zhu and Peng, 2016). ## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.86976.3.sa1](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.86976.3.sa1)

In principle a very interesting story, in which the authors attempt to shed light on an intriguing and poorly understood phenomenon; the link between damage repair and cell cycle re-entry once a cell has suffered from DNA damage. The issue is highly relevant to our understanding of how genome stability is maintained or compromised when our genome is damaged. The authors present the intriguing conclusion that this is based on a timer, implying that the outcome of a damaging insult is somewhat of a lottery; if a cell can fix the damage within the allocated time provided by the "timer" it will maintain stability, if not then stability is compromised. If this conclusion can be supported by solid data, the paper would make a very important contribution to the field.

However, the story in its present form suffers from a number of major gaps that will need to be addressed before we can conclude that MASTL is the "timer" that is proposed here. The primary concern being that altered MASTL regulation seems to be doing much more than simply acting as a timer in control of recovery after DNA damage. There is data presented to suggest that MASTL directly controls checkpoint activation, which is very different from acting as a timer. The authors conclude on page 8 "E6AP promoted DNA damage checkpoint signaling by counteracting MASTL", but in the abstract the conclusion is "E6AP depletion promoted cell cycle recovery from the DNA damage checkpoint, in a MASTL-dependent manner". These 2 conclusions are definitely not in alignment. Do E6AP/MASTL control checkpoint signaling or do they control recovery, which is it?

Also, there is data presented that suggest that MASTL does more than just controlling mitotic entry after DNA damage, while the conclusions of the paper are entirely based on the assumption that MASTL merely acts as a driver of mitotic entry, with E6AP in control of its levels. This issue will need to be resolved.

and finally, the authors have shown some very compelling data on the phosphorylation of E6AP by ATM/ATR, and its role in the DNA damage response. But the time resolution of these effects in relation to arrest and recovery have not been addressed.

Revised manuscript:

I think the authors did a good job in revising the paper, and provide compelling support for a timer function in the checkpoint. I do think they still have missed one important point how MASTL could act as a timer to control recovery. The data clearly show that MASTL somehow controls ATM/ATR activity, whilst their final model (fig.9) places MASTL upstream of CDK activity, without mentioning its feedback on ATM/ATR. I think there are 2 possible explanations for the timer function of MASTL they have discovered here, both may be relevant. The first is enhanced CDK activation by direct control of CDK phosphorylation through MASTL/B55/PP2A. The second is through MASTL-mediated shut-down of ATM/ATR activation (mechanism to be determined) which is also reported here. Their final model and discussion do not display sufficient appreciation for this latter option, and I would argue that the HU-recovery experiment shown in Fig.5B is actually in strong support of the second explanation, rather than the first.

This manuscript describes a role for the ATM-E6AP-MASTL pathway in DNA damage checkpoint recovery. claims.claim: The N-terminus of E6AP co-immunoprecipitates MASTL.

claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C showing MASTL binding to the N3 segment (aa 108-280) of E6AP, and is explicitly stated in the text.

claims.claim: Re-expression of exogenous E6AP reverses the augmentation of MASTL level caused by E6AP gene deletion.

claims.claim: E6AP depletion increases the protein stability of MASTL.

claims.claim: E6AP overexpression reduces the protein stability of MASTL.

claims.claim: E6AP depletion disrupts MASTL ubiquitination in HeLa cells.

claims.claim: E6AP mediates the ubiquitination of MASTL.
claims.source: Furthermore, E6AP depletion disrupted MASTL ubiquitination in HeLa cells (Figure 4G), indicating that E6AP mediated the ubiquitination of MASTL.

claims.claim: E6AP depletion does not further increase MASTL level in cells treated with MG132.

claims.claim: An in vitro ubiquitination assay confirms MASTL as an effective substrate of E6AP.

claims.claim: MASTL ubiquitination is specifically mediated by E6AP in the in vitro ubiquitination assay.
claims.source: MASTL ubiquitination was specifically mediated by E6AP in the assay (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C); the MASTL mutant deleted of the E6AP-binding motif was not ubiquitinated (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro ubiquitination data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C showing MASTL ubiquitination only when E6AP is present, and is explicitly stated in the text.

claims.claim: The MASTL mutant deleted of the E6AP-binding motif is not ubiquitinated.
claims.source: MASTL ubiquitination was specifically mediated by E6AP in the assay (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C); the MASTL mutant deleted of the E6AP-binding motif was not ubiquitinated (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro ubiquitination data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D showing no ubiquitination of ΔN MASTL (lacking E6AP-binding domain), and is explicitly stated in the text.

claims.claim: MASTL depletion substantially hinders DNA damage recovery.
claims.source: MASTL depletion substantially hindered DNA damage recovery, whereas E6AP knockout (KO) accelerated mitotic entry after DNA damage (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by mitotic index data in Figure 5A showing reduced mitotic entry in MASTL knockdown cells after etoposide release, and is explicitly stated in the text.

claims.claim: E6AP knockout accelerates mitotic entry after DNA damage.
claims.source: MASTL depletion substantially hindered DNA damage recovery, whereas E6AP knockout (KO) accelerated mitotic entry after DNA damage (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by mitotic index data in Figure 5A showing increased mitotic entry in E6AP KO cells after etoposide release, and is explicitly stated in the text.

claims.claim: The recovery of mitotic entry in E6AP KO cells is disrupted by MASTL downregulation.
claims.source: The recovery of mitotic entry in E6AP KO cells was disrupted by MASTL downregulation, indicating its dependence on MASTL (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by mitotic index data in Figure 5A showing reduced mitotic entry in E6AP KO cells when MASTL is knocked down, and is explicitly stated in the text.

claims.claim: MASTL depletion causes prolonged cell cycle arrest after HU treatment.
claims.source: MASTL depletion caused prolonged cell cycle arrest; loss of E6AP promoted cell cycle recovery; and suppression of MASTL in E6AP-deleted cells abrogated cell cycle progression (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by FACS data in Figure 5B showing prolonged G2/M arrest in MASTL knockdown cells after HU release, and is explicitly stated in the text.

claims.claim: Loss of E6AP promotes cell cycle recovery after HU treatment.
claims.source: MASTL depletion caused prolonged cell cycle arrest; loss of E6AP promoted cell cycle recovery; and suppression of MASTL in E6AP-deleted cells abrogated cell cycle progression (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by FACS data in Figure 5B showing faster cell cycle progression in E6AP KO cells after HU release, and is explicitly stated in the text.

claims.claim: Suppression of MASTL in E6AP-deleted cells abrogates cell cycle progression after HU treatment.
claims.source: MASTL depletion caused prolonged cell cycle arrest; loss of E6AP promoted cell cycle recovery; and suppression of MASTL in E6AP-deleted cells abrogated cell cycle progression (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by FACS data in Figure 5B showing impaired cell cycle progression in E6AP KO cells when MASTL is knocked down after HU release, and is explicitly stated in the text.

claims.claim: MASTL knockdown does not significantly disrupt cell proliferation under the unperturbed condition.
claims.source: By comparison, MASTL knockdown did not significantly disrupt cell proliferation under the unperturbed condition (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by cell proliferation data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A showing similar cell numbers in control and MASTL knockdown cells without DNA damage, and is explicitly stated in the text.

claims.claim: E6AP knockout in HEK293 cells reduces DNA damage checkpoint signaling after DOX treatment.
claims.source: Interestingly, KO of E6AP in HEK293 cells reduced DNA damage checkpoint signaling, measured by phosphorylation of SMC1, CHK1, CHK2, H2AX, and pan-ATM/ATR substrates after DOX treatment (Figure 5C), and by phosphorylation of pan-ATM/ATR substrates after ETO (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 5C showing reduced phosphorylation of checkpoint proteins in E6AP KO cells after DOX treatment, and is explicitly stated in the text.

claims.claim: E6AP knockout in HEK293 cells reduces DNA damage checkpoint signaling after ETO treatment.
claims.source: Interestingly, KO of E6AP in HEK293 cells reduced DNA damage checkpoint signaling, measured by phosphorylation of SMC1, CHK1, CHK2, H2AX, and pan-ATM/ATR substrates after DOX treatment (Figure 5C), and by phosphorylation of pan-ATM/ATR substrates after ETO (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B showing reduced phosphorylation of ATM/ATR substrates in E6AP KO cells after ETO treatment, and is explicitly stated in the text.

claims.claim: A similar deficiency of ATM/ATR-mediated phosphorylation is observed in HeLa cells with E6AP gene deletion.

claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 5D showing reduced phosphorylation of ATM/ATR substrates in E6AP KO HeLa cells after ETO treatment, and is explicitly stated in the text.

claims.claim: The deficiency of ATM/ATR-mediated phosphorylation in E6AP KO HeLa cells is rescued by E6AP re-expression.

claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 5D showing restored phosphorylation of ATM/ATR substrates when HA-E6AP is re-expressed in E6AP KO cells, and is explicitly stated in the text.

claims.claim: ATM/ATR-mediated substrate phosphorylation in E6AP KO cells is restored by MASTL depletion.

claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 5E showing restored phosphorylation of ATM/ATR substrates in E6AP KO cells when MASTL is knocked down, and is explicitly stated in the text.

claims.claim: E6AP promotes DNA damage checkpoint signaling by counteracting MASTL.
claims.source: Interestingly, ATM/ATR-mediated substrate phosphorylation in E6AP KO cells was also restored by MASTL depletion, indicating that E6AP promoted DNA damage checkpoint signaling by counteracting MASTL (Figure 5E).
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that MASTL depletion rescues checkpoint signaling defects in E6AP KO cells, as shown in Figure 5E and stated in the text.

claims.claim: Co-immunoprecipitation of E6AP with CFP-MASTL is profoundly disrupted by HU treatment.

claims.claim: The loss of E6AP and MASTL association after DNA damage is a result of active DNA damage signaling.

claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data in Figure 6B showing preserved E6AP-MASTL binding when caffeine is added with HU, and is explicitly stated in the text.

claims.claim: Inhibition of ATM/ATR by caffeine preserves E6AP and MASTL association in the presence of HU.
claims.source: This loss of E6AP and MASTL association was a result of active DNA damage signaling, as inhibition of ATM/ATR by caffeine preserved this protein association in the presence of HU (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data in Figure 6B showing preserved E6AP-MASTL binding when caffeine is added with HU, and is explicitly stated in the text.

claims.claim: E6AP possesses a single evolutionally conserved serine, Ser-218 in humans, as a potential consensus site of ATM/ATR-mediated phosphorylation.

claims.claim: E6AP Ser-218 phosphorylation is documented in multiple proteomic databases.

claims.claim: E6AP Ser-218 phosphorylation is induced after HU treatment.

claims.claim: E6AP Ser-218 phosphorylation is induced after DOX treatment.

claims.claim: The phospho-E6AP Ser-218 signal is absent in E6AP KO cells.

claims.claim: The phospho-E6AP Ser-218 signal is diminished with S218A mutation.

claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 7E showing no phospho-E6AP Ser-218 signal in S218A mutant, and is explicitly stated in the text.

claims.claim: Inhibition of ATM using a selective kinase inhibitor reduces E6AP Ser-218 phosphorylation after DOX treatment in HeLa cells.

claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 7C showing reduced phospho-E6AP Ser-218 signal when ATM inhibitor is added with DOX in HeLa cells, and is explicitly stated in the text.

claims.claim: Inhibition of ATM using a selective kinase inhibitor reduces E6AP Ser-218 phosphorylation after DOX treatment in HEK293 cells.

claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B showing reduced phospho-E6AP Ser-218 signal when ATM inhibitor is added with DOX in HEK293 cells, and is explicitly stated in the text.

claims.claim: ATM is the primary kinase to mediate E6AP Ser-218 phosphorylation in response to HU.

claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C showing reduced phospho-E6AP Ser-218 signal when ATM inhibitor is added with HU, and is explicitly stated in the text.

claims.claim: The phospho-mimetic mutant form of E6AP, E6AP S218D, exhibits significantly reduced association with MASTL compared to WT E6AP.

claims.claim: The phospho-mimetic mutant form of E6AP, E6AP S218D, exhibits significantly reduced association with MASTL compared to S218A E6AP.

claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data in Figure 7D showing reduced MASTL binding to S218D E6AP compared to S218A, and is explicitly stated in the text.

claims.claim: DNA damage disrupts MASTL association with WT E6AP.

claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data in Figure 7E showing reduced MASTL binding to WT E6AP after DOX treatment, and is explicitly stated in the text.

claims.claim: DNA damage does not disrupt MASTL association with E6AP S218A.

claims.claim: S218A mutation prevents MASTL protein accumulation after DNA damage.

claims.claim: Cells expressing S218A E6AP exhibit defective DNA damage checkpoint recovery compared to cells expressing WT E6AP, as measured by cell cycle profiling after HU.

claims.evidence: The claim is supported by FACS data in Figure 8B showing delayed cell cycle progression in cells expressing S218A E6AP after HU release, and is explicitly stated in the text.

claims.claim: DNA damage-induced MASTL upregulation is caused by decreased protein degradation.

claims.claim: MASTL degradation is inhibited upon DNA damage as a result of the dissociation of E6AP from MASTL.

claims.claim: E6AP depletion promotes cell cycle recovery from the DNA damage checkpoint in a MASTL-dependent manner.

results.result: MASTL protein levels are upregulated within hours after DNA damage treatment across multiple cell lines (HEK293, SCC38, HeLa) and DNA damaging agents (DOX, HU, CPT, IR).
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C7 collectively demonstrate MASTL upregulation across multiple cell lines and DNA damage agents using immunoblotting. The data show consistent upregulation patterns with appropriate loading controls (α-tubulin, β-actin), supporting the robustness of this observation.

results.result: DNA damage-induced MASTL upregulation occurs concurrently with ATM/ATR activation and is not caused by completion of DNA repair, as evidenced by persistent phosphorylation of RPA, H2AX, and ATM/ATR substrates.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C10 are supported by immunoblotting data showing concurrent MASTL upregulation and persistent DNA damage markers. The temporal correlation between MASTL upregulation and active DNA damage signaling is clearly demonstrated.

results.result: DNA damage-induced MASTL upregulation is unique among mitotic kinases, as other mitotic kinases (CDK1/cyclin B, Aurora A, Aurora B, PLK1) do not show similar upregulation after DNA damage.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C14 and C81 are supported by immunoblotting data showing no upregulation of other mitotic kinases after DNA damage treatment. This specificity strengthens the significance of MASTL upregulation and distinguishes it from general mitotic kinase regulation.

results.result: ATM/ATR activation acts upstream of MASTL upregulation, as caffeine treatment (ATM/ATR inhibitor) abrogates HU-induced MASTL upregulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C15-C16 are supported by immunoblotting data showing that caffeine blocks MASTL upregulation. However, caffeine is a non-specific inhibitor that affects multiple kinases beyond ATM/ATR, which introduces some uncertainty about the specificity of this pathway. More specific ATM/ATR inhibitors would strengthen this conclusion.

results.result: MASTL upregulation after DNA damage occurs at the post-translational level through decreased protein degradation, not through increased transcription.
results.evaluation: Claims C17-C18 and C82 are supported by RT-PCR data showing no significant change in MASTL mRNA levels and cycloheximide chase experiments demonstrating increased protein stability. The combination of transcriptional and protein stability data provides strong evidence for post-translational regulation.

results.result: Exogenous MASTL expressed from a different promoter undergoes similar upregulation after DNA damage, occurring concurrently with ATM/ATR substrate phosphorylation.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C20 are supported by immunoblotting and immunofluorescence data showing that exogenous CFP-MASTL exhibits similar upregulation patterns. This control experiment strengthens the conclusion that regulation occurs post-translationally rather than at the transcriptional level.

results.result: DNA damage treatment (CPT in HeLa cells, HU in SCC38 and HEK293 cells) increases MASTL protein stability and prolongs its half-life.
results.evaluation: Claims C21-C23 are supported by cycloheximide chase experiments showing slower MASTL degradation after DNA damage. The experiments include appropriate controls and quantification, providing strong evidence for increased protein stability as the mechanism of MASTL upregulation.

results.result: E6AP (encoded by UBE3A) is the founding member of the HECT-domain ubiquitin ligase family and was identified as a potential MASTL binding partner through proteomic analysis.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C26 are supported by citations to established literature and a previous proteomic study. These claims provide important background context for the E6AP-MASTL interaction studies.

results.result: E6AP associates with MASTL through direct protein-protein interaction, as demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation, pulldown assays, and in vitro binding of purified proteins.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C29 are supported by multiple complementary approaches (co-IP, pulldown with recombinant protein, and purified protein binding). The convergence of evidence from different experimental methods provides strong support for a direct E6AP-MASTL interaction.

results.result: The N-terminal region of MASTL (mediating E6AP binding) and the N-terminal region of E6AP (aa 208-280, mediating MASTL binding) are responsible for the E6AP-MASTL interaction.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C33 are supported by domain mapping experiments using protein segments in both HeLa cells and Xenopus egg extracts. The bidirectional mapping approach strengthens the identification of interaction domains.

results.result: E6AP regulates MASTL protein levels: E6AP depletion increases MASTL protein without affecting mRNA, E6AP overexpression reduces MASTL, and E6AP knockout augments MASTL in a manner reversed by E6AP re-expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C38 are supported by multiple complementary approaches (siRNA, overexpression, CRISPR knockout, and rescue experiments). The consistency across different experimental methods and the rescue experiment provide strong evidence for E6AP-mediated regulation of MASTL protein levels.

results.result: E6AP modulates MASTL protein stability: E6AP depletion increases MASTL stability while E6AP overexpression reduces it.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C40 are supported by cycloheximide chase experiments with quantification. The bidirectional effects (depletion vs. overexpression) strengthen the conclusion that E6AP directly regulates MASTL protein stability.

results.result: E6AP is the E3 ubiquitin ligase that mediates MASTL ubiquitination and degradation, as demonstrated by reduced MASTL ubiquitination in E6AP KO cells, in vitro ubiquitination assays, and requirement for the E6AP-binding domain.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C46 and C83 are supported by cellular ubiquitination assays, in vitro reconstitution experiments, and domain deletion studies. The combination of cellular and biochemical evidence, along with the specificity controls (MG132 treatment, domain deletion), provides strong support for E6AP as the E3 ligase for MASTL.

results.result: E6AP and MASTL have opposing effects on DNA damage checkpoint recovery: MASTL depletion hinders recovery while E6AP knockout accelerates it, and the E6AP knockout effect depends on MASTL.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C52 are supported by mitotic index measurements and FACS cell cycle profiling after DNA damage. The epistasis experiment (E6AP KO + MASTL KD) demonstrates that E6AP's effect on checkpoint recovery is mediated through MASTL, providing strong mechanistic insight.

results.result: MASTL knockdown does not significantly disrupt cell proliferation under unperturbed conditions.
results.evaluation: Claim C53 is supported by cell proliferation data showing similar growth rates. This control experiment is important for demonstrating that MASTL's role is specific to DNA damage recovery rather than general cell proliferation.

results.result: E6AP promotes DNA damage checkpoint signaling by counteracting MASTL: E6AP knockout reduces checkpoint signaling (phosphorylation of SMC1, CHK1, CHK2, H2AX, ATM/ATR substrates) in a MASTL-dependent manner, and promotes cell cycle recovery.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C59, C85-C86 are supported by immunoblotting data showing reduced checkpoint markers in E6AP KO cells and rescue by either E6AP re-expression or MASTL depletion. The epistasis analysis provides strong evidence that E6AP's effect on checkpoint signaling is mediated through MASTL regulation.

results.result: DNA damage disrupts the E6AP-MASTL association in an ATM/ATR-dependent manner, as HU treatment reduces co-immunoprecipitation and caffeine (ATM/ATR inhibitor) preserves the interaction.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C62 and C84 are supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments. However, the reliance on caffeine as an ATM/ATR inhibitor introduces some uncertainty due to its non-specificity. More specific inhibitors would strengthen this conclusion.

results.result: E6AP contains a conserved serine at position 218 (Ser-218) that represents a potential ATM/ATR phosphorylation consensus site (SQ motif), and this phosphorylation has been documented in multiple proteomic databases.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C64 are supported by sequence alignment data and citations to multiple proteomic studies. This provides strong bioinformatic and literature support for E6AP Ser-218 as an ATM/ATR target site.

results.result: E6AP is phosphorylated at Ser-218 by ATM after DNA damage (HU or DOX treatment), as demonstrated by a phospho-specific antibody and ATM inhibitor experiments.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C71 and C87 are supported by immunoblotting with a custom phospho-specific antibody, validated by absence of signal in E6AP KO cells and S218A mutant, and reduced by ATM inhibitor. The antibody validation and pharmacological inhibition provide strong evidence for ATM-mediated phosphorylation.

results.result: E6AP Ser-218 phosphorylation regulates E6AP-MASTL association: the phospho-mimetic S218D mutant shows reduced MASTL binding, and DNA damage disrupts WT E6AP-MASTL association but not S218A mutant association.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C75 and C88 are supported by immunoprecipitation experiments with phospho-mutants. The use of both phospho-mimetic (S218D) and phospho-deficient (S218A) mutants, along with DNA damage treatment, provides strong evidence that Ser-218 phosphorylation regulates the E6AP-MASTL interaction.

results.result: E6AP S218A mutation prevents MASTL protein accumulation after DNA damage, indicating that Ser-218 phosphorylation is required for MASTL stabilization.
results.evaluation: Claims C76 and C89 are supported by immunoblotting data showing no MASTL increase in cells expressing S218A E6AP after DNA damage. This result logically follows from the persistent E6AP-MASTL association observed with the S218A mutant.

results.result: E6AP Ser-218 phosphorylation is required for timely DNA damage checkpoint recovery: cells expressing S218A E6AP show defective recovery (reduced mitotic entry, delayed cell cycle progression, reduced CDK substrate phosphorylation) and elevated DNA damage signaling compared to WT E6AP.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C80 and C90 are supported by multiple complementary assays (mitotic index, FACS, CDK substrate phosphorylation, checkpoint marker phosphorylation). The consistency across different readouts provides strong evidence that Ser-218 phosphorylation is functionally important for checkpoint recovery.

results.result: ATM/ATR-dependent signaling initiates cell cycle recovery while activating the DNA damage checkpoint, creating a timer-like mechanism that ensures the transient nature of checkpoint arrest through the ATM-E6AP-MASTL axis.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C92 represent the central model of the paper, integrating findings from multiple experiments. The model is well-supported by the data showing that ATM phosphorylates E6AP, leading to E6AP-MASTL dissociation, MASTL stabilization, and checkpoint recovery. However, C92 contains some speculative elements about the 'timer-like mechanism' that, while reasonable, extend beyond direct experimental evidence.

results.result: DNA damage activates ATM and ATR kinases, which phosphorylate and activate checkpoint kinases CHK1 and CHK2, which in turn inhibit CDC25 to prevent CDK activation.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C95 represent established knowledge about DNA damage checkpoint signaling, supported by citations to foundational literature. These claims provide necessary background context.

results.result: MASTL is an important mitotic regulator that is activated during mitotic entry and promotes mitosis by phosphorylating ENSA and ARPP19, which inhibit PP2A/B55 phosphatase, though mitotic entry can still occur in MASTL-depleted cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C102 represent established knowledge about MASTL function in mitosis, supported by multiple citations. These claims provide essential background for understanding MASTL's role in the current study.

results.result: MASTL is required for cell cycle recovery from DNA damage checkpoint in Xenopus egg extracts and promotes cell proliferation under DNA damage in human cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C103-C106 are supported by citations to previous studies from the same research group. These claims provide important background establishing MASTL's role in checkpoint recovery, which motivated the current mechanistic study.

results.result: E6AP mutations cause Angelman syndrome in humans, and mouse embryo fibroblasts lacking E6AP exhibit multiple oncogenic phenotypes including escape from replicative senescence, proliferation under stress, anchorage-independent growth, and enhanced tumor growth in vivo.
results.evaluation: Claims C107-C111 are supported by citations to established literature. These claims provide important context for understanding E6AP's biological significance and potential tumor suppressor function.

results.result: The oncogenic phenotypes of E6AP-deficient mouse embryo fibroblasts can potentially be attributed to MASTL upregulation.
results.evaluation: Claim C112 is speculative and represents a hypothesis rather than a tested result. While the current study shows that E6AP regulates MASTL, the connection to the previously observed oncogenic phenotypes of E6AP-deficient cells has not been experimentally tested. This would require additional experiments to validate.

results.result: ATM-mediated MASTL upregulation may provide an initial signal to trigger positive feedback reactions that shift the balance from cell cycle arrest to recovery.
results.evaluation: Claim C113 is speculative and represents a proposed model. While the data support ATM-mediated MASTL upregulation and its role in checkpoint recovery, the specific mechanism involving positive feedback loops has not been directly tested. This remains a reasonable hypothesis requiring further experimental validation.

results.result: The timer-like mechanism involving ATM-E6AP-MASTL can contribute to the transient nature of the DNA damage checkpoint observed in yeast, frog, and mammalian cells.
results.evaluation: Claim C114 is supported by the experimental data showing that ATM activation simultaneously initiates checkpoint signaling and checkpoint recovery mechanisms. The citations to previous observations of transient checkpoint arrest in multiple organisms provide additional support, though the specific contribution of the MASTL pathway to this phenomenon in different organisms has not been directly tested.

results.result: The impact of MASTL upregulation on promoting checkpoint recovery and cell cycle progression can be attributed to inhibition of PP2A/B55, though additional mechanisms are not excluded.
results.evaluation: Claim C115 is a reasonable inference based on established knowledge of MASTL function (inhibiting PP2A/B55) and the current data showing MASTL's role in checkpoint recovery. However, the specific mechanism by which MASTL promotes checkpoint recovery was not directly tested in this study (e.g., through PP2A/B55 manipulation). The authors appropriately acknowledge that additional mechanisms may be involved.

results.result: MASTL kinase has emerged as an important factor in tumorigenesis and treatment resistance in multiple types of cancer.
results.evaluation: Claim C116 is supported by citations to previous studies and provides important context for the clinical relevance of understanding MASTL regulation.

results.result: MASTL protein levels are upregulated within hours after DNA damage treatment (DOX, HU, CPT, IR) across multiple cell lines (HEK293, SCC38, HeLa). This upregulation is concurrent with ATM/ATR activation and persistent DNA damage markers, is unique among mitotic kinases, and is caused by decreased protein degradation rather than transcriptional changes. The upregulation is abrogated by caffeine treatment, indicating ATM/ATR acts upstream of MASTL stabilization.
results.evaluation: Reviewers raised a critical concern about the timing of MASTL upregulation relative to checkpoint activation. One reviewer explicitly states that the authors claim 'MASTL is not upregulated during the activation stages of the DNA damage checkpoint,' but notes 'their data show otherwise: MASTL upregulation coinciding with RPA phosphorylation and p-ATM/ATR signal.' This temporal ambiguity undermines the interpretation that MASTL acts as a timer for recovery rather than being involved in checkpoint activation itself.

results.result: DNA damage does not induce upregulation of other mitotic kinases (CDK1/cyclin B, Aurora A, Aurora B, PLK1) in HeLa and SCC38 cells, distinguishing MASTL's response from other cell cycle kinases.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge this finding. The editor notes the study identifies 'proteins important for this decision' and reviewers accept that MASTL upregulation is 'unique among mitotic kinases,' implicitly supporting the specificity of MASTL's response compared to other mitotic regulators.

results.result: MASTL upregulation after DNA damage occurs at the post-translational level through increased protein stability rather than transcriptional changes. This is demonstrated by unchanged mRNA levels, similar upregulation of exogenous MASTL, and prolonged protein half-life in cycloheximide chase experiments.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge the mechanism of MASTL stabilization. The editor acknowledges the mechanism is 'supported by solid but not conclusive data,' and reviewers accept that MASTL regulation occurs through protein stability changes, as this is central to the E6AP ubiquitination story that follows.

results.result: E6AP is identified as a binding partner of MASTL through proteomic analysis, with the interaction confirmed by co-immunoprecipitation, pulldown assays, and direct protein binding. The N-terminal region of MASTL (binding E6AP) and aa 208-280 of E6AP (binding MASTL) mediate this interaction.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge the E6AP-MASTL interaction data. The identification of E6AP as the E3 ligase is accepted as part of the 'solid' evidence base, and the mapping of interaction domains is treated as supporting detail for the mechanism.

results.result: E6AP mediates MASTL ubiquitination and degradation. E6AP depletion or knockout increases MASTL protein levels and stability without affecting mRNA, while E6AP overexpression reduces MASTL levels and stability. E6AP depletion disrupts MASTL ubiquitination, and in vitro assays confirm MASTL as an E6AP substrate.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge the E6AP-mediated ubiquitination and degradation of MASTL. This is accepted as part of the core mechanism, with the editor noting the mechanism is 'supported by solid but not conclusive data' overall, but not specifically questioning the E6AP-MASTL ubiquitination relationship.

results.result: MASTL depletion hinders DNA damage checkpoint recovery (reduced mitotic entry, prolonged arrest), while E6AP knockout accelerates recovery. The enhanced recovery in E6AP KO cells is MASTL-dependent, as MASTL knockdown in E6AP KO cells abrogates the accelerated recovery. MASTL knockdown does not affect proliferation under unperturbed conditions.
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge the revised manuscript provides 'compelling support for a timer function in the checkpoint.' While initial concerns existed about whether E6AP/MASTL control checkpoint activation versus recovery, the authors' revisions appear to have addressed this sufficiently for reviewers to accept the recovery function, though one reviewer notes the model still doesn't fully appreciate MASTL's feedback on ATM/ATR.

results.result: E6AP knockout reduces DNA damage checkpoint signaling (phosphorylation of SMC1, CHK1, CHK2, H2AX, ATM/ATR substrates) after DNA damage in both HEK293 and HeLa cells. This deficiency is rescued by E6AP re-expression and by MASTL depletion, indicating E6AP promotes checkpoint signaling by counteracting MASTL.
results.evaluation: This is the central point of contention in the reviews. Reviewers explicitly note the contradiction: 'The authors conclude on page 8 "E6AP promoted DNA damage checkpoint signaling by counteracting MASTL", but in the abstract the conclusion is "E6AP depletion promoted cell cycle recovery from the DNA damage checkpoint, in a MASTL-dependent manner". These 2 conclusions are definitely not in alignment.' One reviewer states the major issue 'whether the E6AP-MASTL pathway mediates checkpoint activation or checkpoint recovery was not experimentally addressed' and notes 'MASTL upregulation coinciding with RPA phosphorylation and p-ATM/ATR signal' contradicts the authors' interpretation.

results.result: DNA damage disrupts the E6AP-MASTL interaction, as shown by reduced co-immunoprecipitation after HU treatment. This dissociation is dependent on active DNA damage signaling, as caffeine (ATM/ATR inhibitor) preserves the interaction in the presence of HU, leading to inhibition of MASTL degradation.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge the observation that E6AP-MASTL interaction is disrupted by DNA damage. This is accepted as part of the mechanism linking ATM/ATR activation to MASTL stabilization, with reviewers noting 'very compelling data on the phosphorylation of E6AP by ATM/ATR.'

results.result: E6AP is phosphorylated at Ser-218 by ATM after DNA damage. This site is evolutionarily conserved, documented in proteomic databases, and phosphorylation is induced by HU and DOX treatment. The phospho-specific signal is absent in E6AP KO cells and diminished with S218A mutation. ATM inhibition reduces this phosphorylation.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly praise this finding, noting 'very compelling data on the phosphorylation of E6AP by ATM/ATR, and its role in the DNA damage response.' The identification and characterization of the Ser-218 phosphorylation site is accepted as solid evidence.

results.result: E6AP Ser-218 phosphorylation is required for E6AP-MASTL dissociation and MASTL stabilization. The phospho-mimetic S218D mutant shows reduced MASTL binding compared to WT or S218A. DNA damage disrupts MASTL association with WT E6AP but not S218A. The S218A mutation prevents MASTL accumulation after DNA damage.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge the functional consequences of Ser-218 phosphorylation on E6AP-MASTL interaction and MASTL stability. This is accepted as part of the mechanism linking ATM activation to MASTL stabilization through E6AP phosphorylation.

results.result: Cells expressing the non-phosphorylatable E6AP S218A mutant exhibit defective DNA damage checkpoint recovery (reduced mitotic entry, delayed cell cycle progression, reduced CDK substrate phosphorylation) and elevated DNA damage signaling compared to cells expressing WT E6AP.
results.evaluation: While reviewers acknowledge the S218A data, one reviewer notes a critical concern: 'the time resolution of these effects in relation to arrest and recovery have not been addressed.' The elevated checkpoint signaling in S218A cells could indicate either defective recovery or enhanced checkpoint activation, and the temporal relationship remains unclear, relating back to the central ambiguity about whether this pathway controls activation versus recovery.

results.result: The ATM-E6AP-MASTL axis constitutes a timer-like mechanism where ATM/ATR signaling, while activating the DNA damage checkpoint, simultaneously initiates cell cycle recovery. This ensures the transient nature of the checkpoint, with ATM-mediated MASTL upregulation potentially triggering positive feedback reactions that shift the balance from arrest to recovery.
results.evaluation: This is the central interpretive claim that reviewers find problematic. While one reviewer states the revised manuscript provides 'compelling support for a timer function,' another notes the authors 'still have missed one important point how MASTL could act as a timer to control recovery' and that 'their final model and discussion do not display sufficient appreciation' for MASTL's feedback on ATM/ATR. The reviewer argues 'the HU-recovery experiment shown in Fig.5B is actually in strong support of' MASTL-mediated shutdown of ATM/ATR rather than just CDK activation. The timer model is accepted as plausible but incompletely supported.
